title: It's Never Too Late to Start Again
description: Urban College honors Denella Clark with the Robert M. Coard Leadership Award—and celebrates her mother, Pastor Pearline James, who earned her Urban College degree at age 60. A new scholarship will help immigrant women pursue education later in life.
content:
At this year's commencement ceremony, Urban College of Boston will recognize Denella Clark with the Robert M. Coard Leadership Award and an honorary Human Services degree. Clark credits her passion for community service to her mother, Urban College alumna Pastor Pearline James.

Pastor Pearline James achieved her degree goal later in life, graduating from Urban College at age 60 after decades of community care work. Originally from Jamaica, she moved to Boston with her family in 1971 and settled in Mattapan, where she became known as a caregiver, mentor, and community leader.

In conversation with Urban College President Dr. Yves Salomon-Fernández, Denella reflected on the values that shaped her: “We are a people of resilience, we are people of faith.” She explained that philanthropy means “the love of humanity, or the love of humankind.”

Denella's 35-year career in philanthropy and nonprofit leadership has included roles with NBC Universal, the Red Cross, the Louis D. Brown Peace Institute, and the NAACP. The leadership skills that define her professional life began at home, watching her mother care for others.

In 2024, Denella and her family established the Loving Gestures Fund in Pastor James' name. She is now creating the Pastor Pearline James Scholarship Fund at Urban College to assist immigrant women pursuing education later in life, with an initial goal of $10,000 and hopes to endow it permanently.

“This institution opened doors for my mother,” Denella shared. Through this scholarship, her mother's legacy will continue opening doors for future Urban College students—proof that educational opportunity has no age limit.

title: Certificate, Associate's Degree, or Bachelor's Degree? Which Degree Type Is Right for Me?
description: Certificate, associate, or bachelor's? The right choice depends on your goals, timeline, and how education fits your life. Here's how to choose the credential that's right for you.
content:
Choosing to return to school brings both excitement and uncertainty. Whether you're seeking advancement in your current role, changing careers, or formalizing existing work experience, selecting among credential types can feel daunting. There's no single “right” answer—the best path depends on your unique circumstances and professional aspirations.

Certificate Programs: Quick Wins for Career Growth

Certificates emphasize applied, job-ready skills over extended academic requirements. They typically take one year to complete and appeal to professionals seeking momentum rather than lengthy commitments. Urban College's certificates can later be applied toward associate degrees, allowing learners to build progressively rather than restart. The Elder Care Certificate, for example, requires 21 credits and prepares students for roles like community health workers, who earn an average of $55,090 a year in Massachusetts (BLS).

Associate Degrees: Building Stronger Foundations

Typically two-year programs, associate degrees combine technical expertise with broader academic skills including communication and analytical reasoning. They increase earning potential beyond certificates and provide a foundation for a future bachelor's degree, with credits often transferring to four-year institutions. Urban College's Human Services Associate Degree prepares students for roles such as case-management assistants and community outreach workers; the field shows about 8% projected growth in Massachusetts.

Bachelor's Degrees: Planning for Leadership

Four-year degrees target higher-level roles and leadership positions. Transfers from certificates or associate degrees can accelerate completion and reduce both time and expense. Urban College partners with institutions offering transfer pathways to facilitate smooth credit transitions.

Why Urban College Works for Adult Learners

All programs operate fully online and asynchronously, accommodating working professionals with family obligations. Eight-week accelerated sessions enable flexible pacing, and credit stacking lets learners progress from certificates through associate and bachelor's degrees—each level building on the last. The right educational path meets you where you currently stand while supporting movement toward your goals.

title: Am I Ready for College? How to Know if Now is the Right Time
description: Going to college for the first time—or returning after a pause—can feel overwhelming. Here's how to know if now is the right time, and how Urban College supports you every step of the way.
content:
Going to college for the first time, or returning after a long pause, can feel overwhelming. How do you know if you're ready? At Urban College of Boston, we believe you belong here. Everyone deserves the opportunity to learn more, earn more, and pursue a career that brings financial stability and economic mobility.

College is a big decision, and it's normal to have questions. Each semester, you'll enroll alongside an advisor who will guide you through your options, help you plan your schedule, and ensure you're on track to reach your goals.

Before You Apply

To apply to Urban College, you'll need a high school diploma, GED, or equivalent credential. If you've completed coursework outside the United States, our enrollment specialists will help review your transcripts and determine whether credits may transfer. A 3-credit course typically requires about nine hours of dedicated time per week—manageable for most students, even when taking multiple courses.

Is Urban College Right for You?

Urban College may be a great fit if you are a recent high school graduate unsure about a traditional four-year college, working while earning your degree, a multilingual student who wants to study in both your native language and English, looking to improve your English, or concerned about the cost of college. Most of our students graduate debt-free through grants, scholarships, and other financial assistance—and many don't pay anything upfront.

Flexible Course Schedules Built for Real Life

We offer both 16-week semesters and accelerated 8-week terms, with asynchronous, synchronous, hybrid, and flex-online formats so you can choose the pace that works best for you.

Student Success: The Heart of Urban College

The Learning Resource Center offers tutoring, technology assistance, English placement support, and professional-skills workshops. We also connect students with resources for housing, transportation, health services, immigration support, and food assistance. If you're questioning whether you're ready for college, that might be the clearest sign that you are—you don't need to have it all figured out. You belong at Urban College.

title: A New Pathway for Community Health Workers at Urban College of Boston
description: Urban College is now a Massachusetts-approved Community Health Worker training site, letting students earn a certificate and prepare for CHW licensure at the same time—cutting required experience hours in half.
content:
Urban College of Boston is now licensed by the Massachusetts Department of Public Health as an approved Community Health Worker (CHW) training site. This milestone strengthens the institution's commitment to workforce development and expands students' access to meaningful, community-centered careers.

Urban College's Elder Care Certificate now includes embedded, license-track CHW training as a core component. CHW training is also available as an optional track within the Children's Behavioral Health Certificate and as an elective within Human Services programs. Students can earn their certificate and prepare for CHW licensure simultaneously, reducing required work-experience hours by 50%.

Community Health Workers are trusted community members who help high-risk patients improve health outcomes by connecting them with hospital, home-, and community-based services. Their work includes advocacy and case management, developing care plans, conducting needs assessments with medical teams, facilitating access to social services, and supporting families in problem-solving.

Demand for licensed CHWs is growing across Massachusetts and the United States, particularly in multilingual and historically underserved communities. Because CHW services may be reimbursed by Medicare, hospitals and community-based health organizations are increasingly hiring for these roles.

Urban College's CHW training is accessible as a standalone professional pathway, embedded within the Elder Care Certificate, as an optional track within the Children's Behavioral Health Certificate, as an elective within Human Services programs, or through workforce-development cohorts. Employers can also launch customized cohorts tailored to their workforce needs.

title: 2026 Commencement Speaker and Honorees: A Celebration of Leadership, Service, and Community
description: Urban College will celebrate its 2026 graduates on May 30th with keynote speaker Lincoln C. Mali and honoree Denella J. Clark at the Emerson Cutler Majestic Theater.
content:
On Saturday, May 30th in Downtown Boston, Urban College will hold its commencement ceremony at the Emerson Cutler Majestic Theater, honoring leaders whose work transforms lives and strengthens communities.

Lincoln C. Mali — Keynote Speaker

Lincoln C. Mali, the keynote speaker, will also receive an honorary degree in Human Services. He currently serves as CEO for Southern Africa at Lesaka Technologies, a fintech company expanding financial access to underserved consumers and merchants. He previously held senior leadership roles at Standard Bank Group, is the founding president of the Association of South African Payment Providers, and authored “Blazing a Trail: Lessons for African Leadership.” “I believe deeply in the power of education to transform lives, families, and entire communities,” Mali said.

Denella J. Clark — Honorary Degree Recipient

Denella J. Clark, president and CEO of the Boston Arts Academy Foundation, will receive the Robert M. Coard Leadership Award and an honorary degree in Human Services. A Jamaican immigrant and Hyde Park resident, Clark has dedicated her career to philanthropy, equity advocacy, and youth development. Her connection to Urban College is personal—her mother, Pastor Pearline B. James, was an alumna. “This institution opened doors for my mother, and her journey continues to inspire the work I do every day,” Clark reflected.

Celebration Details

The festivities begin at 12:30 p.m. with a lion dance performance led by the Gund Kwok Asian Women's Lion and Dragon Troupe, processing from Urban College's campus to the theater. The formal ceremony begins at 1:00 p.m.

title: Urban College Blog | Urban College of Boston
description: Urban College of Boston alumni often have one powerful thing in common: they are deeply mission-driven and as they rise, they lift others with them. That mission-driven spirit is central to the work o...
content:
Urban College of Boston alumni share a common characteristic: they are deeply mission-driven and help lift others as they advance. That spirit is exemplified by Charmaine Burrell's journey from Human Services student to social-work leader. When women receive education, she notes, entire families and communities benefit.

Uplifting Communities Around the World

Charmaine is completing her Master of Social Work at Bridgewater State University and joined a study-abroad program in South Africa and Istanbul. In Durban, she worked with the Family Literacy Project during a 17-day cohort focused on literacy, social work, and community organizing. Her team transported more than 800 pounds of hygiene supplies, books, and classroom materials, and monetary donations purchased groceries and offset government funding cuts.

From Human Services to Social Work

Charmaine began her education in 2009 while working as a paraprofessional with Boston Public Schools and raising her family. She enrolled in Urban College's Human Services Associate Degree and graduated in 2011. The flexible evening schedule let her balance full-time work, parenting, and studies. “I knew this was for real,” she recalled. “I was ready to commit.”

Education That Moves With You

After graduating, Charmaine planned a one-year break before her bachelor's degree—a pause that lasted a decade until 2021, when she enrolled at Bridgewater State. All of her Urban College credits transferred, including electives. She graduated in 2024, then began Bridgewater's MSW program with a Social Justice Award scholarship. She now works at Foxborough High School as an Instructional/Social Work Assistant, supporting students returning to school after mental-health hospitalizations.

Advocacy to Remove Barriers

A self-described “policy person,” Charmaine has served as a student ambassador for the Massachusetts Social Work Student Association, supporting licensure equity, youth-justice reform, and food-insecurity efforts. She plans to begin a clinical internship and is considering a Doctor of Social Work program.

The Power of Empathy

Reflecting on Urban College, Charmaine returns again and again to empathy—centering humanity in every interaction. Her path reflects Urban College's mission: expanding access to education that supports personal growth, professional advancement, and community impact.

title: Urban College Blog | Urban College of Boston
description: For many adults, college doesn’t look the same as it used to. Many of today’s college students are balancing full-time jobs and family care with their coursework, or they’re returning to college after...
content:
For many adults, college doesn't look the same as it used to. Today's students are often balancing full-time jobs and family care with coursework, or returning after years away to finish their degrees. Online learning has become a respected, flexible, and accessible pathway—according to NCES, 53.4% of students were enrolled in at least one online course in Fall 2023, a 12% jump from pre-pandemic levels.

Flexibility That Supports Your Life

Urban College offers multiple learning formats so students can choose what fits their schedule: asynchronous courses you access anytime, live synchronous classes, hybrid courses, flex-online courses, and accelerated 8-week sessions. Students who aren't ready for a full degree can start with a career-focused certificate and apply those credits toward an associate degree later.

Affordability That Removes Barriers

Online study saves on transportation, parking, childcare, and housing. Tuition is $317 per credit with no hidden costs—no textbook fees, no tech fees. Most Urban College students pay little or nothing out-of-pocket thanks to financial aid and scholarships, and payment plans make costs manageable.

Certificates and Degrees Designed for Real Careers

Every program is built to help students move forward—gaining in-demand skills, strengthening resumes, and advancing careers while continuing to work. Many students start with a certificate to build momentum, then continue to an associate or bachelor's degree with ongoing support.

Support Systems to Help You Succeed

Student support is built into everything Urban College does: tutoring online and in person, multilingual support services, career counseling and resume assistance, and student groups and events. “I always give Urban College credit for being where I am today,” says alum Adzele B.

Choosing an online program doesn't mean choosing less—it means choosing an educational pathway that fits your responsibilities, schedule, and goals.

content:
Urban College of Boston recently hosted the Light of Opportunity Celebration, bringing together new supporters, longtime advocates, partners, and community members. The gathering reinforced the institution's commitment to expanding educational access, strengthening workforce-aligned programs, and creating clear pathways for adult learners.

Several speakers shared remarks: Dr. Yves Salomon-Fernández, President, discussed the urgency and optimism guiding the college's future; Joan Becker, Board Chair, underscored leadership's dedication to student success; Tom O'Brien, Foundation Chair, stressed how philanthropic support removes barriers for adult learners; and Kristin McSwain, Director of the Mayor's Office of Early Childhood, connected early education, workforce development, and family stability in Boston. Urban College alumna Krystal Ray Jackson shared her personal journey, demonstrating what opportunity truly looks like when obstacles diminish.

The evening reflected collective enthusiasm and shared confidence in student potential. A significant development emerged: Dr. Connee Counts offered a $100,000 matching-gift challenge for contributions submitted by December 31st, effectively doubling every donation.

title: Urban College Blog | Urban College of Boston
description: For the past several years, it’s been nearly impossible to escape headlines claiming that AI is coming to replace us all and that no job is safe. With so many companies and products now promoting thei...
content:
For the past several years, it's been nearly impossible to escape headlines claiming that AI is coming to replace us all. There's no denying AI is transforming certain industries and automating repetitive tasks—but many careers can't be automated.

As Urban College Board Member Joan Becker puts it, the jobs that will remain in the age of AI are “deeply human and require skills like critical thinking, empathy, [and] commitment to justice.” These are skills no algorithm can replicate, and Urban College prepares students for exactly these kinds of roles.

What AI Can't Replace

According to Forbes, “jobs involving high human interaction and judgment tend to have the lowest automation risk.” Careers in caregiving, behavioral support, and education require trust, human connection, and the ability to navigate complex emotional dynamics. AI might help with documentation or scheduling, but it can't form a bond with a child, comfort a grieving family, or advocate for a patient.

Human-Centered Career Programs

Urban College offers programs that prepare students for essential, human-centered careers—Early Childhood Education, Human Services, Social Work, Elder Care, Behavioral Health, and Paraprofessional Education—available online and in multiple languages. These are also among the fastest-growing careers in the country: social and human-service roles are projected to grow 6% by 2034, community health workers 11%, and home health and personal care aides 17%.

Advancing Equity in the Age of Automation

Urban College serves multilingual learners, parents, and working adults who are often overlooked in traditional higher education—offering asynchronous courses, academic and career support, and wraparound services. Students can complete fast-track certificates, stack credits toward associate degrees, and transfer to bachelor's programs through university partnerships.

While AI and automation continue to evolve, it's empathy, care, and human connection that will define the future—and Urban College is preparing students for careers only humans can do.

title: Urban College Blog | Urban College of Boston
description: Urban College of Boston is proud to announce a new partnership with the City of Boston that brings professional development opportunities to grassroots organizations making a difference in the lives o...
content:
Urban College of Boston has announced a partnership with the City of Boston to support grassroots organizations serving young people. Through the City's Youth Development Fund, the college will provide professional development to 21 emerging nonprofit organizations in the Emerging Organization Learning Community.

Participants will take online courses covering fundraising, nonprofit management, governance, and board and staff development, supplemented by in-person collaboration sessions for Boston's youth-serving leaders. “We welcome the opportunity to support the organizations and leaders of the Emerging Organization Learning Community, whose work reflects the diversity and resilience of our city,” said Dr. Yves Salomon-Fernández, president of Urban College.

The City's Youth Development Fund awarded $1,512,163 to 127 nonprofit organizations serving youth and young adults. José F. Massó, City of Boston Human Services Chief, noted that the Learning Community gives emerging leaders an opportunity to build community while strengthening their management and leadership skills. The kickoff event was held at the Teen Center at St. Peter's.

title: Urban College Blog | Urban College of Boston
description: Did you know that Urban College of Boston has a podcast?   We are proud to introduce  Your Seat at the Table , a new podcast hosted by Urban College President Dr. Yves Salomon-Fernández. Each conversa...
content:
Urban College of Boston has launched Your Seat at the Table, a podcast hosted by President Dr. Yves Salomon-Fernández that explores the experiences of alumni, faculty, staff, and community leaders—and how higher education shapes lives and transforms careers.

Featured Episodes

Episode 1: Jerrell Cox — Legacy, Leadership, and the Power of Higher Education. The CEO of United South End Settlements shares his 30-year journey, which began as a camper at the organization. His advice: “The time is now. Don't wait. It's a journey, and be gentle with yourself, but the most important part is starting.”

Episode 2: Sherene Clayton — Discipline, Calculated Risks, and Starting Small. A Partner at Northwestern Mutual, Sherene compares investing to athletic training and encourages listeners to define their goals, take calculated risks, and run their own race.

Episode 3: Anna Berry — From Head Start to Higher Ed. Urban College's Vice President of Student Success reflects on her path from first-generation college student to educator: “We are never fully formed. That idea is exciting to me.”

New episodes feature guests including Martha Niño, a first-generation Mexican-American tech entrepreneur, and Leslie Forde, a researcher supporting working mothers.

Watch and subscribe on YouTube →

title: Urban College Blog | Urban College of Boston
description: Just before graduating with honors from Urban College of Boston in May 2025, Krystal Jackson Ray found herself reflecting on her journey while traveling on a family vacation.&nbsp;&nbsp;  “I w...
content:
Just before graduating with honors from Urban College of Boston in May 2025, Krystal Jackson Ray reflected on her journey while on a family vacation, drawing parallels between the resilience of historical figures and her own path: “If she could do that, I could finish my degree.”

Krystal's first attempt at higher education ended in disappointment. As a first-generation student managing single motherhood and grief from losing her mother, she found traditional college inflexible and withdrew. Years later, while working in Applied Behavior Analysis with children, a parent recognized her potential and encouraged her to pursue teaching—sparking her aspiration to become a special-education teacher.

She enrolled at Urban College after a professional-development course through Neighborhood Villages. Her first semester was challenging—managing ADHD, work, and family—and she considered withdrawing again. Instead, she reached out to the Student Success office, where connecting with VP of Student Success Anna Berry, also a first-generation college student, proved transformative. “It meant so much to me that she shared her own story,” Jackson Ray explained. The Learning Resource Center provided the academic support that helped her excel.

This May, Krystal graduated with her Early Childhood Education Associate Degree with honors. Urban College's flexible online structure was crucial—balancing full-time work, motherhood, church ministry, and community advocacy would have been impossible otherwise. She is now pursuing additional certificates before attending Lesley University to complete her bachelor's in Early Childhood Education with a family-services concentration.

Her ultimate vision is to open a community center serving families and children with exceptional needs—honoring her mother's legacy and addressing a gap in early-intervention services. As the mother of two neurodivergent children, she feels uniquely equipped to create individualized plans that support development. Her story is a testament to transformation through perseverance.

title: Urban College Blog | Urban College of Boston
description: Sometimes, the best journeys begin with a change of scenery.&nbsp;  That was certainly the case for one of our remarkable graduates, Elijah Watts, who found his way to Urban College of Boston afte...
content:
Sometimes, the best journeys begin with a change of scenery. That was certainly the case for Urban College of Boston graduate Elijah Watts, who found his way to the institution after an unsteady start to college during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Craving something new and encouraged by friends already in Boston, he made the move north. One day, while waiting at a T-stop, he spotted an Urban College poster that piqued his interest—and that curiosity quickly turned into action. He enrolled in the General Studies Associate Degree program with the goal of becoming a meteorologist. “I've always been fascinated by weather, tornadoes especially. And I love geography… how landscapes and climate work together. It's where my heart is.”

Urban College's flexible, mostly asynchronous online classes turned out to be a perfect fit, and accessible technology like Brightspace helped him stay on track. The supportive environment was the true standout: he formed a strong connection with his advisor, Kendall Driscoll, and the Executive in Residence course gave him new confidence in networking, building a résumé, and envisioning his future.

Graduating with honors this May, Elijah is heading to Kennesaw State University in Georgia as a junior majoring in Geography, already thinking ahead to a master's degree and possibly a PhD in Earth and Atmospheric Sciences. Despite his ambition, he stays grounded—noting that everyone is on their own path, and different paces are equally valid.

content:
Urban College President Yves Salomon-Fernández delivered a touching and inspiring TEDxBabsonCollege talk titled “Unlocking Human Potential”—all about the power and importance of community.

People are empowered to tap into their potential when we have support, safety, and access to opportunity. Each one of us has potential; it just needs to be validated and achieved. Communities are made up of individuals, and just one person can help another discover and seize their capabilities.

“My community helped me develop my confidence. They taught me how to network, how to advocate for myself and for others. They helped me navigate and thrive in the workplace. They created the environment where I could succeed and learn from my failures. They helped me see my own potential, and turn that potential into reality. Now, this is the power of community.”

We are so proud to have Yves at the helm of Urban College of Boston. Her advocacy, leadership, and empathy inspire our faculty, staff, and students daily. At Urban College, we know that support and community are integral to a successful college journey—every interaction is an opportunity to create a ripple effect that can change a student's life for the better.

title: Meet Your Professor: Elizabeth Maglio
description: A passionate educator and advocate for social justice   Since joining Urban College in 2014, Elizabeth Maglio has been a tireless educator and policy advocate, weaving real-world lessons from her dive...
content:
Since 2014, Elizabeth Maglio has served as a dedicated educator and policy advocate at Urban College, bringing lessons from her work at community nonprofits and her role as a town councilor in Braintree into her classroom.

Her connection to Urban College began while she worked at a community multi-service nonprofit in Roxbury/Dorchester. Witnessing the transformative impact of Urban College educators teaching Early Childhood Education courses on-site inspired her to join as an adjunct professor. “The mission of Urban College is incredible. The fact that it was born out of an anti-poverty nonprofit is unique,” she says.

She has taught Intro to English, College Writing, Health & Wellness, and psychology courses, and helped develop the college's virtual curriculum when the pandemic shifted learning online. She values online accessibility, noting it “empowers students to learn in their personal ideal environment” while preparing them for the technology economy.

A cornerstone of Maglio's teaching is a commitment to social justice. Her Cultural Competency course draws on her nonprofit background and elected service to facilitate dialogue about community challenges. In one assignment, students track their carbon footprints for a week; in another, she introduces JR's border-wall art installation, challenging students to use creativity for social change.

Maglio expresses profound respect for Urban College's students—primarily first-generation students, women, and non-native English speakers—who often juggle caregiving, full-time work, and their education. She celebrates the moment “when their lightbulb moment hits in class” and sees opportunities open before their eyes.

description: Joan Becker replaces Peter Ebb who served as Urban College’s Board Chair for nearly 15 years; Amelia Manning appointed Vice Chair &nbsp;...
content:
After nearly 15 years of leadership, Peter Ebb has stepped down as Board Chair at Urban College of Boston. Joan Becker, retired vice provost for academic support services and undergraduate studies at the University of Massachusetts Boston, succeeds him. Amelia Manning, chief operating officer at Southern New Hampshire University, will serve as Vice Chair, and Ebb will remain on the board.

During his tenure, Ebb oversaw the College's response to the COVID-19 pandemic, including securing approval from the New England Commission of Higher Education to offer online courses. “Peter has given so many of his talents, skills, passion, and heart to Urban College and the academy for decades,” said President Dr. Yves Salomon-Fernández.

Becker brings extensive experience advancing educational equity; throughout her 20-year career at UMass Boston she led academic programs and student services including general education, advising, career services, and disability services. “We are not just opening doors to education; we are creating pathways to upward mobility that will uplift entire communities,” she said.

Manning has spent her 20-year career at SNHU ensuring the institution executes its vision and mission. “By continuing to align our programs with workforce needs in industries such as early childhood education and human services, we are not only preparing our students for meaningful careers but also contributing to the economic future of our city and state,” she said. The appointments come as Urban College continues serving its diverse student body as a Hispanic-Serving Institution and an AANAPISI, offering programs in English, Spanish, Mandarin, Portuguese, and Haitian Creole.
